candidates.title: Expertise changed how clinicians responded to wrong neonatal-imaging AI advice
candidates.event_date_reason: The journal record identifies 20 October 2026 as the online publication date.
candidates.source_date_reason: Date shown on the Nature journal record and accepted-article metadata.
candidates.what_changed: A peer-reviewed multi-reader crossover study reported that reader expertise modified reactions to deliberately wrong AI suggestions for neonatal pneumoperitoneum, with residents accepting 52.0% of erroneous suggestions while three neonatologists overrode 91.7%.
candidates.why_now: The article was published on 20 October inside the initial 72-hour discovery window and adds direct, bounded human-AI interaction evidence rather than another model-only benchmark.

underlying_identity.cohort: 125 external neonatal abdominal radiographs from 11 South Korean tertiary hospitals; 14 readers

scope_fit.ai_connection: Reader behaviour under reliable and deliberately erroneous diagnostic-AI advice in neonatal radiography.
scope_fit.reader_consequence: Clinical-AI teams can treat interface design, training and sentinel behaviour as measurable safety controls rather than assuming model accuracy determines safe use.

deduplication.archive_coverage: Inspected all merged HealthTech ledgers and stories through 20 October, current main and the canonical 21 October branch/PR namespace. No prior story or candidate with this DOI, cohort or event identity was found.

candidates.reason: Select as bounded human-factors evidence: a peer-reviewed crossover reader study directly measured responses to correct and deliberately wrong AI suggestions, while wording remains limited to the simulated study and its small reader subgroups.

evidence.publication_status: Peer-reviewed npj Digital Medicine article published online 20 October 2026; accepted early version inspected with a full supplementary PDF.
evidence.study_design: Multi-reader crossover diagnostic study with unaided, reliable-AI and deliberately error-injected AI conditions; 1,750 interpretations across 14 readers and 125 radiographs.
evidence.validation_setting: Retrospective external radiographs from 11 South Korean tertiary hospitals, interpreted in a study interface rather than live clinical care.
evidence.independent_validation: The reader set and images were external to model training, but the evaluation was author-run; no independent replication or live-site implementation study was reported.
evidence.funding: Reported support from Asan Medical Center, the Korea Health Industry Development Institute and the National Research Foundation of Korea; funders were reported to have no role in study conduct or reporting.
evidence.conflicts_of_interest: The article reports no competing interests. The inspected code repository is author-maintained and marked for research/education, not clinical use.
evidence.corrections_retractions: No correction or retraction notice was identified on the inspected article, supplement or repository during the bounded 21 October review.
contradictory_findings: Adjusted interaction tests support different condition effects by reader group, but individual post-hoc contrasts were wide and not significant after multiplicity correction.
The study found expertise-related resistance to erroneous AI advice, not proof that any AI-assisted workflow improves neonatal outcomes or routine diagnostic safety.
limitations: Only 14 readers participated: six paediatric radiologists, three neonatologists and five radiology residents; subgroup estimates are imprecise and the neonatologist finding is hypothesis-generating.
The study was retrospective and simulated, with 125 selected images and no measurement of downstream treatment decisions, patient outcomes or harms.
All images came from South Korean tertiary hospitals; generalisability to other settings, devices, prevalence and reader mixes is unknown.
The error-injection condition isolates automation bias but does not reproduce the full pattern of failures or interface constraints of a deployed product.
evidence.applicability: Useful for designing training, interfaces and escalation around diagnostic AI. It does not justify deploying the research model or extrapolating the observed reader behaviour to other specialties.

claims.supported_statement: In a simulated crossover reader study of 1,750 interpretations, five radiology residents accepted 52.0% of deliberately wrong AI suggestions, while three neonatologists overrode 91.7% of them; the small subgroup finding is hypothesis-generating.
locators: Article abstract, Methods and Results sections: reader composition, 125-case external set, three AI conditions and 1,750 interpretations.
Supplementary Table 7 and sensitivity-analysis text: group-by-condition interaction, multiplicity-adjusted post-hoc uncertainty and leave-one-neonatologist-out results.
claims.evidence_scope: Observed reader responses in this retrospective simulated study only; no live clinical outcome, causal implementation benefit or general cross-specialty effect.
limitations: Reader groups were small and not randomized samples of their professions.
Post-hoc subgroup comparisons were imprecise after correction; neonatologist resistance should not be treated as a population estimate.

verification.checked_by: ChatGPT research assistant (source audit; no human editorial approval)
verification.supported_scope: Full accepted-article text and supplement support the reader counts, study conditions and reported acceptance/override percentages; wording explicitly preserves uncertainty and simulation limits.
verification.reason: Reconciled abstract-level percentages with supplement sensitivity analyses and excluded patient-benefit and deployment claims.

study.design: Multi-reader crossover diagnostic study with unaided, reliable-AI and error-injected AI conditions.
study.setting: Retrospective study interface using external radiographs from 11 South Korean tertiary hospitals.
study.population_or_dataset: 125 neonatal abdominal radiographs: 40 positive and 85 negative under the study reference standard; 14 readers comprised six paediatric radiologists, three neonatologists and five radiology residents.

sample_sizes.reason: External test cases reported in Methods.
Six paediatric radiologists, three neonatologists and five residents.
Total interpretations reported by the article.

study.comparator: Unaided interpretations and reliable-AI suggestions, compared with deliberately error-injected suggestions within the crossover design.
primary_endpoints: Reader diagnostic accuracy and responses to correct versus erroneous AI suggestions across expertise groups.
secondary_exploratory_endpoints: Group-by-condition interactions and leave-one-neonatologist-out sensitivity analyses.

results.endpoint: Acceptance of erroneous AI suggestions among residents
results.uncertainty: Small group of five residents; simulated cases and no population-level confidence interval cited for this descriptive percentage.
results.locator: Abstract and Results section on responses to erroneous suggestions.

results.endpoint: Override of erroneous AI suggestions among neonatologists
results.uncertainty: Wilson 95% CI 83.0% to 96.0%; only three neonatologists, so authors characterize the pattern as hypothesis-generating.
results.locator: Supplement sensitivity analyses and mechanism plot/table for erroneous suggestions.

results.metric: Reader-group by AI-condition interaction p value
results.uncertainty: Individual Holm-adjusted post-hoc contrasts were wide and non-significant.

study.follow_up: Single-session reader experiment; no longitudinal or clinical follow-up.
study.harms: No patient harms were measured because the study did not alter live care.
study.analysis_notes: Percentages describe behaviour under experimentally injected wrong suggestions. They are not the sensitivity or specificity of a marketed device.
study.applicability: Supports attention to expertise, training and sentinel behaviour when testing AI-assisted diagnosis; does not establish clinical effectiveness.

rationales.significance: Direct evidence about automation bias and expert sentinel behaviour is consequential for diagnostic-AI safety, but the experiment did not change care.
rationales.claim_support: Peer-reviewed full text and supplement support the central measurements; very small reader subgroups cap confidence.
rationales.relevance: Highly relevant to clinicians, implementers and safety teams evaluating AI-assisted diagnosis.
rationales.material_change: New peer-reviewed multi-reader evidence with an error-injection condition and subgroup analyses.
rationales.durability: Human-factors and evaluation lessons should remain useful beyond this specific model.
